Sweep Backtest (SBT)

5040 optimizer configurations over one FIXED curation (data/cbt_3yr_v30_evrank) · no LLM, no re-curation · knobs from investor_profile.backtest.md

1. Parameter settings

The 5 FREE swept knobs — every combination is a cell, 8×7×5×3×6 = 5040 configs — and the values considered. These knobs only RE-WEIGHT a fixed set of curator picks, which is what makes the grid free: no LLM call is made and no event is discovered or closed differently. The last two rows are the exceptions, and the cost column says why. max_events (panels 11–12) and min_bundle_articles (panel 13) are CURATION knobs: the first decides which events stay live and so which tickers ever reach the optimizer, the second decides which bundles the scout is shown as a company’s news. Neither can be replayed — every value needed its own full re-curation and its own LLM bill. Every other optimizer / curator parameter is held at its investor_profile.backtest.md value.

2. Return vs drawdown

The horizontal axis is max drawdown — the book's biggest peak-to-trough loss as a fraction of its running peak; further right = deeper loss. The vertical axis is annualized return, so upper-left is best. Each point is one config; colour is capital hit-rate — the share of exposure that sat in tickers which ended profitable. It was cancellation until 2026-08-22, but cancellation is 83% return across the grid, so it merely recoloured the y-axis. Hit-rate is +0.45, independent enough to add a third dimension: a dark point in the upper-left earned its return WITHOUT the money sitting in winners, which is luck rather than picking. The live config is the magenta ★ star. Amber squares are its 22-cell region; violet squares are the region of the best-scoring config (24 · 0.25 · 30 · 4 · 12.0), which is what table 10 now ranks by worst member. The two sets are disjoint here — no cell belongs to both — so reaching the top of the grid is more than a one-knob move.

These are RAW per-config values. Table 9 reports the median across each config’s 22-cell neighbourhood, so a point here and its row there are not the same number. The raw cloud is kept on purpose: regional medians would shrink the visible spread to 63–83% of the truth, and adjacent regions share 24 of 25 members, so smoothing would draw 5,040 points that are ~95% the same data as their neighbours. The rings are how the good neighbourhoods stay visible without flattering the picture — they sit at the EDGE of the cloud, not in its dense middle, which is exactly why dispersion hides them.

3. Return vs Sharpe

The same cloud with Sharpe on the horizontal — return per unit of volatility, one of the two measures table 10 ranks on. This is the one panel here where upper-RIGHT is best, since higher Sharpe is better; every other risk axis on this page reads the other way. Colour is risk aversion (λ, the optimizer’s own setting) — dark is timid. It is an INPUT, not an outcome, so it explains the cloud rather than re-describing it, and it is orthogonal to return on this grid (+0.21). If the good cells are uniformly dark the ranking is buying safety rather than skill; if they span the ramp, it is not. The cloud is a tight rising diagonal — return and Sharpe correlate +0.92 across the grid, so for most configs they say the same thing and there is no return/risk trade to agonise over. The divergence is all in the tail, which is exactly where a config gets picked. On this book the grid's biggest final value ($409,784, 107%/yr) ranks only 137 of 5,040 by Sharpe because it earns that return on a 55% drawdown. The best-Sharpe cell (1.59) makes $212,565 on a 28% drawdown instead. Read the top-right corner, not the top edge: a point that is high but far left is return bought with volatility a live account has to actually sit through.

4. Return vs cancellation

The fourth view of the same points, and the one that matters most: the horizontal axis is the share of the winners' gains handed back by the losers, so upper-left is best — a book that earns and keeps it. Colour is churn (trades over the run) — dark is heavy trading. Orthogonal to return here (+0.24), so it answers what neither axis can: was this bought with turnover? A pale upper-left point earns well, keeps it, and does so without a deep hole. The cloud's shape is itself the finding: if it were a tight rising diagonal these knobs would only be trading return against cancellation, and it is not one.

5. Return vs second-half slope

Return against when it arrived. The horizontal is the second-half slope — (final − midpoint) ÷ 1.5 years, in dollars per year — so a point far right was still compounding in the back half of the run, and a point at or left of zero made its money early and then coasted or gave it back. Upper-right is best. Colour is safe-park — of the capital that did not end in a winner, the share parked in anchors rather than sunk in a loser. It is the only metric here that is orthogonal to return (-0.07), so it is the one colour that shows something the two axes cannot.

The cloud is a tight rising diagonal — return and slope correlate +0.95, tighter even than return and Sharpe — so for almost every config the two say the same thing. That tightness is the finding, and it is a warning about slope, not a recommendation of it: a measure this correlated with return carries almost no information return does not, which is consistent with slope ranking configs at the 53rd percentile on the re-curation transfer test, i.e. no better than random. Only 0 of 5,040 cells clear 50%/yr while finishing with a negative slope, so the made-it-early-then-coasted failure this panel was built to expose barely happens on this book. 295 cells (6%) do have a negative slope, but they are the low-return cells you would drop anyway.

Two things to read carefully. The axis runs p0.2 to p99.8 of the cells, not the full range — a handful of extremes would otherwise squash the middle 90% into a fifth of the plot. However many cells fall outside is stated in the panel’s top-right corner rather than silently dropped. And the two axes are computed off different equity curves — annualized return compounds rebalance-window to rebalance-window while slope comes from the daily series, which for the live config end at $302,079 and $460,556 respectively. The rank ordering is unaffected, but do not read a ratio off this panel. Violet squares are table 10's LIVE config’s region (amber) — 25 of its 25 members have a positive slope, median $91,641/yr.

6. Return vs capital hit-rate

The share of allocated capital-days that sat in tickers which ended up profitable. Capital-WEIGHTED on purpose: ten winners at 1% and one loser at 40% is not good picking, and an unweighted count would say it was. Colour is risk aversion (λ, the optimizer’s own setting) — dark is timid. It is an INPUT, not an outcome, so it explains the cloud rather than re-describing it, and it is orthogonal to return on this grid (+0.21). If the good cells are uniformly dark the ranking is buying safety rather than skill; if they span the ramp, it is not. — what the winners handed back — so the corner you want is right and pale: the money sat in the right names AND kept the gains.

7. Return vs edge

Dollars earned per unit of exposure: total gain divided by total capital-days. It separates a book that earns a lot by HOLDING a lot from one that earns a lot per dollar-day of risk. Colour is churn (trades over the run) — dark is heavy trading. Orthogonal to return here (+0.24), so it answers what neither axis can: was this bought with turnover? A dark dot far right earns well per unit of exposure without that exposure being in winners — which is luck, not picking.

8. Return vs the pc score of what actually got funded

For every ticker the optimizer funded (weight above 1%), its fractional price change from one rebalance to the next. The horizontal axis is the median of those changes across every ticker and every period, so further right means the money went into tickers whose price was rising. On the live config that median is +4.28%, against +2.70% for the whole watchlist and +0.44% for every ticker the curator declared live that week. Dot colour is how many tickers hold capital at once.

9. Return vs per-curation return (PCR)

The x-axis is PCR — the book’s median percent change from one curation to the next, the quantity CBT panel 2 plots, one number per config. The y-axis is annualized return, as on every scatter above. The two axes are related by construction and measure +0.66 on this grid, so the cloud leans; what the panel is for is the SPREAD around that lean. A cell sitting well above the trend earned its annual return in a few big periods, one below it ground the same return out steadily. Colour is funded names/day, the same channel as panel 8, so the two read as a pair. PCR is a COLUMN in table 10 and does not vote: across three curations its median flips sign, its mean form restates annualized, and its mean-over-noise form measures +0.97 against Sharpe.

10. The best region of the grid

A config’s region is itself plus every config one setting away — 25 in all — and every number here is the median and standard error across them. The score is the mean of the region’s percentile rank on TWO columns — Sharpe and PCR vs SPY; every other column is shown but does not vote. They measure different things: Sharpe is risk-adjustment with no market awareness, PCR vs SPY is portfolio return NET OF THE MARKET. pc-funded voted until 2026-08-29 and no longer does — once the SPY-relative metric is in it carries nothing and past K=16 it costs (mean 78.0 for the pair against 75.8 for all three). Both are picking measures; the SPY-relative one measures picking where the money is. The raw PCR column does not vote either — only the SPY-relative one. PCR is the per-curation return — the book’s median percent change from one curation to the next, the quantity CBT panel 2 plots. Shown, NOT scored: its median flips sign across curations, its mean form restates annualized, and its mean-over-noise form measures +0.97 against Sharpe. PCR vs SPY is the one that votes: the median of the PAIRED per-period differences, book minus SPY. That pairing is what makes it a metric at all — SPY’s median is a single number per curation, so subtracting it from PCR would be a constant offset and reorder nothing (rho 1.0000). Subtracting period by period reorders (rho 0.65–0.76), and adding it lifts out-of-sample selection at every cut size tested, worst pair 31 → 58. Ranking neighbourhoods instead of single cells means a config only wins if the settings around it work too. Sharpe scores 1.95 for the live config against 1.00 for a random book drawn from the same watchlist (scripts/null_book.py), so it is measuring the config and not just the curation it was handed.

Which knobs to move next, and which to leave alone

STALE AS OF 2026-09-01 — read the caveat before the ranking. Everything in this section was measured over four sweeps computed while min_trade_size ran as a POST-FILTER that renormalized the surviving weights to sum to 1, which silently undid concentration_cap on every rebalance. 690 of 774 days sat above a 0.4 cap and 147 of them held a single name at 100%. So the two knobs this ranking places LAST (0.4% and 1.8% of variance) are precisely the two that were disconnected — they measured inert because they WERE inert. The floor is now off and the cap is a box bound the solver enforces exactly. This ranking will be redone against the 13-curation re-sweep; until then treat items 1–5 as history, not advice.

optimizer_lookback_days is now 30, and it was the only knob with real leverage — a variance decomposition of log(final) over the four sweeps on hand gives it 23–44% against 0.4–4.9% for every other knob. The five below are what is left, ranked by the evidence rather than by this table’s score. Each row is the MEDIAN final over 1,800 cells at that level, with lookback held at 30, in each of the four curations — so these are marginals, not single cells.

1. risk_aversion 8 → 12 — the one worth taking. It wins in BOTH monthly curations ($138k vs $125k on v24, $154k vs $133k on v23), which is the cadence this book runs. It loses on biweekly and weekly, so the win is cadence-specific and should be read that way. Second-highest leverage of the remaining five at 4.2%.

2. concentration_cap 0.6 → 0.25 — directional, weaker. Best in three of four curations, but it loses on v24, the newest monthly one, and carries only 1.8% of the variance. Note this REVERSES at the old lookback: at 21 the same comparison favoured 0.6, which is a plain demonstration that these knobs interact and that main effects explain only ~40% of the spread.

3. min_trade_size — SUPERSEDED. Now 0.0 and removed from the grid. The old reading here (0.2 → 0.05, “real and tiny”) had the direction right and the reason wrong. It looked negligible because changing its VALUE barely mattered: at any setting the post-filter renormalized the book into the same few names. The knob was not a small effect, it was the mechanism disabling a different knob. It is also malformed as stated — a box LOWER bound applies to every asset, so it cannot express “hold nothing OR hold at least x”; imposed literally it either goes infeasible (22 names × 0.2 = 4.4 > 1) or forces names to be held at exactly the floor, MANUFACTURING the dust it claims to remove. Enforcing the cap on the same journal moved the book $790k → $158k, so the old headline was earned by breaking the risk control.

4–5. max_watchlist and drop_unfunded_weeks — no signal, do not touch. Their best level differs in every curation (max_watchlist wins are split 6/8/12/16, one each), which is what a knob with no reproducible effect looks like. Moving either would be fitting the draw.

The caution that applies to all five. Every recommendation above is marginal-median evidence, which is what caught lookback correctly after single-cell comparisons got it backwards. But main effects sum to only 39–55% of the variance here; the rest is interaction. Change one knob at a time, rebuild, and re-read this table — a knob that looks good in the margin can reverse once another moves, which is exactly what concentration_cap just did.

11. Which tickers this solution fails on

The 30 tickers that lost the most on average, across every config in the sweep that funded them. Bar length is that average, per book -- summing across cells would add up 7,200 parallel books and mean nothing. Colour is how far the ticker had already run in the 30 days before the book bought it, which is usually the real story: CADL loses in 100% of the configs that fund it and was still a +227% winner over the window the curator held it, because every one of them bought in the same month, right after a 315% jump.

12. Portfolio value vs max_events

The one knob on this page that is not free to sweep. Everything above replays a FIXED curation through different book math, so 5,040 cells cost nothing; max_events decides which events stay live and so which tickers ever reach the optimizer, meaning each point here is a full re-curation ($22.89 and several hours for the series). Bars are final portfolio value and, beside it, the gain on the six no-brainer names from panel 10 — same axis, same unit. The line is the share of events culled at birth — opened and retired without a single agent read, i.e. work paid for and thrown away. Read the CULL LINE first: it is a structural count the cap moves directly, while final value is one lucky name away from noise, and each point is a single stochastic sample (the scout is an LLM; two runs at the same cap would differ). A monotone trend across the six is worth something; a one-point spike in dollars is not.

13. Risk-adjusted quality vs max_events

Sharpe per cap, against the > 0.8 floor the current gate set uses. Read it beside panel 12: a cap that wins on final value while dropping below the floor has not won anything the shortlist would admit. Sharpe is NOT what table 10 ranks by — that is robust, cancellation rank + drawdown rank — and Sharpe measured at the 54th percentile on the re-curation transfer test, i.e. a coin flip. It is kept here as a gate and a sanity column, not as a ranking.

14. Portfolio value vs min_bundle_articles

min_bundle_articles is the fewest articles a company bundle needs before the scout is shown it as that company’s news. Below the floor the bundle is not built and its article falls to the beat or unclustered path — nothing is dropped, only reframed.

15. Portfolio value vs LLM spend

Final portfolio value from eight complete 3-year curations that differ only in event_agent_model, ordered left to right by what that model cost, with wall-clock per curation on the right axis. The shaded band is the measured noise floor: the same settings curated twice finished 1.86× apart.

16. What the money actually buys: decision quality vs spend

Each arm made ~565 keep-or-exit calls over its 3-year curation, graded on three tests: was the catalyst datable, did the write-up claim more than its cited sources establish, did the live/exit call contradict its own stated exit condition. The bar is the share Claude Fable-5 judged clean on all three, estimated from a stratified sample of each arm's calls. The judge saw no prices and no outcomes, and was blind to which model produced the decision.

17. Decision quality, ranked by what the model costs

Panel 17's numbers, arranged to be read on their own: dearest model at the top, cheapest at the bottom, bar length is the share of calls judged clean, and the shade is price — dark is dear. Labels give each model's cost as a multiple of the cheapest arm; the colour bar carries the dollars. If spending more bought better decisions, the dark bars would be the long ones. Six models rather than eight: the two arms that re-ran a model at a different reasoning effort are kept in panels 14, 16 and 17 but dropped here, where they would cost a sentence of explanation without changing the picture.

18. Where each model actually fails

Panel 17's three tests, split out, same estimate. dated is Fable-5's verdict on the catalyst the model chose to open an event on: a specific resolvable event such as a contract award, a ruling or an FDA decision, rather than an open-ended trend like “AI demand grows”. supported is whether the write-up stayed within what its own cited sources establish. consistent is whether that period's live-or-exit call cohered with the model's own stated exit condition — it applies to every call, not only the exits. A call counts as clean in panel 16 only if it passes all three, which is close to but not the product of these bars — the failures overlap, since a vague catalyst tends to come with thin sourcing.

19. The bake-off, in full

Every arm, every measure, ordered by LLM spend. Cancellation, drawdown and Sharpe are book behaviour; dated / supported / clean are decision quality; final value is the number that cannot be trusted alone. Read the last three columns against the first: the correlation between what an arm costs and what its book returns is the thing this table exists to let you check for yourself.
